state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about what changing the heights by cutting the plants in half or growing them by 3 cm would do to the range. Consider how the distance between the tallest and shortest plant would be affected in each scenario. Can you see how changing all values by the same proportion could impact the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if we cut them all in half, like 24 becomes 12 and 42 becomes 21, the difference between them would still be the same because we're dividing everything by 2? But then if we add 3 cm to all of them, that would change the range because we're adding the same amount... wait, no, that doesn't make sense either does it? I'm confused about why one changes it and one doesn't.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with recognizing that changing all values by the same proportion can impact the range. Think about how the size of the changes in each scenario affects the spread of the data. Consider how cutting the heights in half versus adding a fixed amount would alter the range.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: So like... when we cut them in half, we're making the difference smaller because 42 minus 13 is 29, but then 21 minus 6.5 is only 14.5, right? But then when we add 3 to everything, the difference stays 29 because we're adding the same thing to both the biggest and smallest? Is that it?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the proportional change misconception through well-calibrated prompts that lead the student to independently discover that proportional changes affect range while additive changes don't, resulting in clear correction of the original misconception by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher effectively scaffolds by breaking down the problem into conceptual components (proportional vs. additive changes), adjusts support based on student progress, and guides without directly providing answers, though could have been slightly more responsive to the student's specific confusion in Turn 2.
